title: #62 Plan Your Follow-Up Question in Advance
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Barton argues that follow-up diagnostic questions -- asked after a re-explanation to check whether understanding has actually improved -- are too important to be improvised in the moment. He gives two classroom examples of the risk: one where a teacher made up a follow-up question about laws of indices that accidentally worked "either way" (addition or multiplication), so it failed to distinguish whether the student's misconception had actually been resolved; and another where a teacher, after successfully improvising a follow-up on fraction subtraction, simply reverted to asking "does that make sense?" for a different question because he couldn't think of a follow-up on the spot. In a coaching conversation, that teacher admitted the gap wasn't due to lack of planning time but the pressure of the live lesson. Barton's conclusion is that a few extra minutes of planning before the lesson yields a much more reliable diagnostic than trying to invent an equivalent, misconception-targeted question live.
points: Improvised follow-up questions risk failing silently: Barton's indices example accidentally created a question answerable by either the correct or the incorrect method, so it couldn't actually detect whether the misconception was fixed.
When a teacher can't think of a follow-up question live, the fallback is often the low-information "does that make sense?" -- exactly the vague check the follow-up question was meant to replace.

The teacher who couldn't invent a follow-up in the moment admitted he could have thought of one during lesson planning, showing the constraint is live cognitive load, not the underlying difficulty of the question.
Barton's fix is a discipline change, not a technique: build the follow-up question into lesson planning in advance rather than trusting it will surface reliably under the pressure of a live lesson.
quotes: A clear teacher explanation, followed by a re-check for understanding using a question that assesses the same skill, provides much more reliable evidence that our response has had the intended impact than the classic: Does that make sense?
One of the critical misconceptions students have about the laws of indices is knowing whether to add or multiply the powers. With a 2 and 2, you can do it either way and still be correct.
In the heat of a lesson, with many things vying for our limited attention, the chance of us making up as good a follow-up question as we would outside this environment is minimal.
In the coaching session afterwards, I asked him why he did a follow-up question for the fractions question but not one for the Venn Diagrams question.
Creating a follow-up question on the spot may be tempting. But for an extra couple of minutes of planning time, I recommend preparing it in advance.
